articles.title: What we should make of CIA boss John Ratcliffe’s secret trip to Moscow
articles.summary: There is nothing routine about John Ratcliffe making a secret, 10,000-mile return dash to Moscow, writes Frank Gardner.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump said John Ratcliffe's trip to Russia was a "semi-routine" visit but there is nothing routine about the CIA chief making a secret, 10,000-mile return dash to Moscow.

Ratcliffe met Russian intelligence officials on Tuesday - notably his opposite number in Russia's overseas spy agency, Sergei Naryshkin - after arriving unannounced on a US military plane, the Kremlin confirmed.

It's been nearly five years since his predecessor William Burns made this trip and that was at a similarly tense time, just as Russia was drawing up plans to invade Ukraine. So, this is probably serious.

In the absence of any official US comment on the reason for the mission, it is being widely reported Ratcliffe's trip was to warn Moscow not to escalate in relation to the stalemate in Ukraine - possibly by taking action against Nato members.

One US official told Politico that the "meeting was primarily to warn Russia against any escalatory action against the Baltic states".

The UK is also in Russian crosshairs. On Thursday, a foreign ministry spokeswoman said Russia could strike British military targets as retaliation for Ukrainian strikes on Russia using British missiles.

And a drone carrying an explosive which was discovered at an airport in the German city of Leipzig was probably Russian, security experts have said.

News of Ratcliffe's visit follows reports of US intelligence assessments that President Vladimir Putin was planning a limited assault on a Nato ally.

But you don't need the world's most powerful electronic eavesdropping organisation – the US National Security Agency – to know that Putin is under mounting domestic pressure to "do something" to break the deadlock.

Ukraine's deep strikes with long-range drones have not only hammered Russia's energy industry, they have brought the war home to ordinary Russians.

Nothing says things are not going to plan more than long queues for petrol and billowing smoke coming from stricken oil refineries. The Kremlin sees these attacks as Nato fighting an indirect war on Russia by using Ukraine as a proxy.

So how will Russia respond? There is a broad spectrum of possibilities here.

These include stepping up the ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine that Moscow is already launching, including targeting the centre of Kyiv, knowing that Ukraine is running dangerously low on Patriot interceptors to stop them.

UK drone factories may face attacks from 'unknown sources', says former Russian minister

Rosenberg: Shortage of petrol but not patriotism as Russians feel growing impact of war

It could entail expanding the undeclared "hybrid war" that Russia is already suspected of waging against Nato countries, using sophisticated cyber-attacks, drone incursions and using not-so-sophisticated criminals to carry out arson attacks on munitions factories.

But at the even more alarming end of the scale there are other potential scenarios which the Kremlin may be considering, urged on by hardliners.

One is to distract attention from its obvious failure to win the war in Ukraine by testing Nato's resolve through a limited attack on a Baltic state. Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania were all once part of the Soviet Union, effectively ruled from Moscow until 1991.

Today they are all members of Nato, while still being home to substantial Russian-speaking communities.

Putin will be well aware of Donald Trump's periodic disdain for Nato and he may have calculated that a low-key attack on say, Lithuania, is not going to trigger Nato's mutual self-defence clause – Article 5 – and that the US will not respond.

In which case it would make sense for part of the CIA chief's unexplained mission to Moscow was to remind Russia that the US is still fully committed to Article 5.

Lithuania is of special interest to the Kremlin as it has a common border with Poland known as the "Suwalki Gap". Just 60 miles long, this strip of land is all that separates Russia's client state Belarus from its nuclear-armed exclave of Kaliningrad, which is separated from mainland Russia.

If Russia were to seize that it would effectively cut off those three Baltic states by land from their Nato neighbours.

Then there is the question of tactical nuclear warheads. It has long been said that Russian military doctrine views these small but highly destructive weapons as an integral part of its order of battle.

Moscow has been warned off, by friend and foe alike, not to break the 81-year long taboo on using nuclear weapons in anger.

Yet this could still be a tempting option for Vladimir Putin to "escalate to de-escalate" by demonstrating to Ukraine that it has such catastrophic weapons at its disposal it would be better for Kyiv to capitulate to Moscow's terms now or face annihilation.

Of course, in the absence of any clear, attributable, official confirmation from the US as to what this sudden CIA dash to Moscow was all about then it is always possible it was about something else.

That could be trying to persuade Russia to end its military cooperation with Iran, for example, or maybe about more prisoner swaps or the prospect of a mass mobilisation of Russian troops.

But make no mistake, this trip was highly unusual and it came at a time of rising tension between Moscow and the West. Something is almost certainly up.

articles.title: More than 800 missing, including 65 Americans, as Nepal flood deaths mount
articles.summary: More than 1,000 people, including many Americans, are still missing along the Nepal-China border after deadly floods and mudflows likely triggered by a glaci...
articles.body:
Rescue teams were searching for hundreds of missing people along the Nepal-China border Thursday after a catastrophic, deadly torrent of floods and mud swept through several communities a day earlier following a glacial collapse. The head of Nepal's tourism board told CBS News Thursday that 65 U.S. nationals were among those missing in the wake of the disaster.

The Nepal Police reported at least 360 people dead and more than 1,400 are missing in Nepal and Tibet, an autonomous region of China.

Local reports cited the National Emergency Operation Center as saying Thursday the missing included 113 Nepali tourists, 85 security personnel from the army and police as well as 161 residents, as authorities ramped up operations in the worst-affected districts of Nuwakot and Rasuwa.

Chinese state broadcaster CCTV separately reported that 558 people were missing in Tibet — 260 of them foreigners — and two villagers were rescued. At least three people were reported killed as of Thursday morning, it said.

65 Americans missing, Nepal Tourism Board says

Hikmat Singh Ayer, CEO and senior director of the Nepal Tourism Board, told CBS News' Arshad R. Zargar on Thursday that at least 65 Americans were among the missing foreign nationals in the small Himalayan nation, almost doubling the number of U.S. nationals reported missing the previous day.

In a subsequent update, the tourism board said 27 foreign nationals had been rescued from the flood zone in the Rasuwa district, including two U.S. nationals identified as a man and woman in their 50s.

A U.S. State Department spokesperson told CBS News Thursday that the agency was aware of about 90 Americans who may be impacted by the floods, and it was continuing to closely track the situation. The department said Thursday that three U.S. citizens had been safely rescued, and the spokesperson said the agency was not yet aware of any U.S. deaths.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio expressed U.S. solidarity Wednesday with the Nepali people, saying in a social media post that the department "stands ready to support the government of Nepal with needed humanitarian assistance."

In a series of social media posts , the U.S. Embassy in Nepal expressed "heartfelt condolences to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives in the devastating floods" and said it was "working to account for U.S. citizens who may have been affected."

The embassy urged U.S. nationals in the region who were able to contact their families, hotels, guides or trekking or tour companies as soon as possible however they could, but it noted that communications were still severely disrupted.

The U.S. State Department said it was closely monitoring the situation and sending an adviser to the region to help with response efforts, as well as a $500,000 grant to Catholic Relief Services.

U.S. citizen Deepak Dandu said his wife, Sridevi Vejella, is among those missing in Nepal. She had just finished a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, which he said was a "lifelong dream" for her, and was crossing from China into Nepal with the Isha Foundation Trekkers society when the flood hit, he told CBS News. He said the foundation told him that she was part of a group who were present at Gyirong Port immigration complex.

Dandu was getting ready to board a flight to Hyderabad, India, where his son is.

"He is going through a lot, hearing all the news," Dandu said of his son. "I think he is really upset. I'm trying to go there and be with him."

Flash floods decimated villages, slamming into houses, roads, bridges and power plants. Videos broadcast by regional news outlets and posted on social media show violent torrents of water surging through valleys and mountain passes, tearing down bridges and dams and sweeping away buildings.

Drone footage in Nepal on Wednesday showed roads destroyed and buildings buried by thundering water the color of wet cement.

The region's steep valleys are economic lifelines and travel corridors but are precarious when disaster strikes. Images showed what appeared to be the second floors of buildings in Nepal's hard-hit Nuwakot district slathered in mud after the torrent rushed by. Debris hung from tree branches and wires, vehicles were buried and some stunned survivors were caked in mud. The floods halted travel in some areas.

There was little time for anyone to flee.

"When I reached Dhunge bazaar, in half an hour, the flood came and damaged all the market. People were preparing to go to office then," resident Shoyam Rajbhandari said. "How many people are missing or dead, we don't know."

Since early morning, army and private helicopters have been deployed. The Nepalese army rescued more than 100 people from flood-affected areas through helicopter operations Thursday, army spokesperson Brigadier General Raja Ram Basnet said.

At least eight foreign nationals were airlifted to Kathmandu, he said, adding that army teams also evacuated people trapped inside facilities linked to the Trishuli hydropower project.

Rescuers found bodies about 62 miles downstream from the disaster zone in Chitwan district. Dozens of injured people have been transported to the country's capital, Kathmandu, for advanced medical care.

In Tibet, a mudslide that struck near the land border crossing of Gyirong Port on Wednesday left mud in the surrounding areas more than 5 feet deep on average, with some road sections exceeding 6 feet, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported Thursday. Roads leading to the port were all damaged, while communication was cut off, it said. With light rain continuing in the area, secondary collapses or landslides may occur, it added.

CCTV said a barrier lake has also been discovered in the direction of the port, posing challenges to the rescue operation. Chinese authorities deployed a large military transport aircraft to send a team to the region, it said.

Officials in Nepal had earlier said hundreds of foreigners were reported missing, including Indian nationals on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus.

Buddhist spiritual leader the Dalai Lama said Thursday that he was praying for all those killed in devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet, French news agency AFP reported. "I pray for all those who have lost their lives, and offer my sympathy and heartfelt condolences to the bereaved and to all those affected by this tragedy," he said in a statement.

Glacier collapse, not earthquake, seen as catastrophe's cause

The U.S. Geological Survey first reported a magnitude 4.4 earthquake early Wednesday, about 41 miles north of Kathmandu, near the border. The USGS later updated its analysis to say the seismic event it measured was a magnitude 5.2 glacial collapse that sent debris flowing downstream with catastrophic impact on communities. It said its determination was based on data from nearby seismic stations, long period seismic waves and satellite imagery, and that no earthquake had occurred.

Climate experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development said an avalanche from a glacier likely caused Wednesday's flash flood.

"Hydrological observations indicate the exceptional speed and magnitude of the flood wave," they said in an emailed statement, noting that water levels at one point on the Trishuli River rose by as much as 27 feet over half an hour.

The Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi, had maximum flooding, they said.

Climate change's threat to region increasing

"The Lhende Khola has flooded twice in 14 months, this time triggered by an ice rock avalanche from a glacier on the Nepal side that blocked the river and released a sudden surge downstream," said Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at the climate research group.

He noted the importance of early warnings in "a warming Himalaya."

The disaster in Nepal and Tibet is not a one-off. The Lhende Khola river system has now flooded twice in just 14 months and the increasingly unstable Himalayan ice system threatens communities, infrastructure and water supplies across one of the world's most densely populated regions.

It saw similar flash floods in August last year, when a glacial lake in Tibet overflowed because of high temperatures. Nine people were killed, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting Nepal and China, was damaged.

The Himalayan mountain range spans several countries in South Asia and has many of the world's highest peaks and remaining glaciers.

The steep slopes and the lush valleys below the Himalayan mountain range are especially vulnerable to flooding and landslides, and extreme weather events like intense monsoons and melting glaciers have become more common because of warming due to human-caused climate change .

Researchers in Kathmandu found earlier this year that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region are melting faster, with ice loss rates doubling since 2000.

The threat from melting glaciers has become a global concern.

articles.title: Ratko Mladić: BBC correspondent on meeting dangerous fanatic early in Bosnian war
articles.summary: BBC special correspondent Allan Little met the "Butcher of Bosnia" in the early months of the Bosnian war.
articles.body:
Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladić, dubbed the "Butcher of Bosnia" for his actions during the Balkan wars of the 1990s, has died in prison.

BBC special correspondent Allan Little was there throughout the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, and met Mladić in the early months of the Bosnian war.

At night, you could watch the fires of ethnic cleansing across the landscape. The flames provided the only light under the night sky and the black valley would glimmer with flecks of orange.

You could watch the men of our village move about silently in the shadows of their homes, each armed with some ancient weapon salvaged from wars long ago and, like the fears and the suspicions and the distrusts, handed down through the generations.

One morning I watched a procession of men and women emerge from a forest. They had been driven from their homes two days earlier and had fled with what they could carry.

Most were on foot. Some were crammed into the back of ancient farm vehicles drawn by donkeys. There were perhaps 40,000 of them. Their home town had fallen to a Serb advance that had come without warning.

Among them, one man seemed close to collapse. He stopped to speak to us.

The whole town had fled, he said. He had become separated from his wife in the long trek to safety and was now worried that she had not made it. His pale, almost translucently white skin was stretched across the bones of his face like parchment. His forehead was livid blue from a fall.

I asked him how old he was. He said he was 80. "May I ask" I said, "are you a Croat or a Muslim?"

The memory of it shames me even now as I hear, in my mind, his answer echo down the years.

Our convenient ethnic shorthand reduced them to Serbs, Croats and Muslims. But they were also musicians and scientists and doctors and plumbers and farmers and mothers and fathers and brothers and sisters and very often children.

I met Mladić in that first hot summer of the war in Bosnia. We were at Lukavica barracks on the southern edge of Sarajevo. The barracks was awash with weapons and the menacing strut of the paramilitaries.

You could buy a Kalashnikov for 200 dollars, a hand grenade for just one dollar – the same price, I would soon learn, as the cost of a fresh egg in the besieged city.

I shook his hand and he held it fast and pulled me in close. He told me he had just come back from the Sarajevo city centre front line and I saw that he was pumped up by the exhilarating proximity of the fighting.

He held my hand for many minutes, fixed me with his eye and told me he was the great defender of brotherhood and unity in former Yugoslavia, and that he dreamed of a world in which there would no guns and no war. He struck me then as fanatical, dangerously so.

In the years that lay ahead, forces under his command committed the worst war crimes on European soil since the Nazis. They bequeathed to the lexicon of war a grim new euphemism - ethnic cleansing. They committed mass murder, extermination, mass rape, forced expulsions. They burned village after village, all in the name of creating an ethnically put Serbian territory in Croatia and Serbia. Ultimately, at Srebrenica, they committed genocide.

Two days after I had met the old musician on that damp muddy roadside, I found myself drawn into the passions of the war in a personal and – at the time – devastating way.

My cameraman, Tihomir Tunukovic, a man I had known and worked alongside during the previous 18 months, was killed by a Serb gunner on a ridge above the road he was driving on. We had parted earlier that morning. He was 25 years old, a talented and ambitious young film maker from Zagreb.

We drove his body back along the rutted mountain pathways to the coastal city of Split. We broke our hearts at his funeral. The grief of it connected us to the sentiments of the war – the impulse to vengeance and counter vengeance – that were so much a feature of what we were witnessing.

General Mladić did not pull the trigger but his command created an atmosphere of wanton permissiveness which cost tens of thousands of lives.

articles.title: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle hit out at Meta after £13 billion child harm settlement, slam ‘data-extraction business model’: ‘The company paid to avoid yet another trial’
articles.summary: UK News: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have once again put the spotlight on children's online safety. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have criticised Meta's \"d.
articles.body: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have once again put the spotlight on children's online safety. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have criticised Meta's "data-extraction business model" after the company agreed to pay up to £13 billion to settle a major child harm lawsuit in the US.In a statement cited by The Daily Mail, the couple accused Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, of having used the model "on our children and all users for years". Meta is led by chairman and chief executive officer Mark Zuckerberg.Harry and Meghan said the settlement meant Meta had "paid to avoid yet another trial outcome that would force it into accountability". They also argued that the company could afford the payout, claiming reports estimate Meta will make the equivalent of the settlement amount back in profits within 30 days.The agreement ends a legal battle in the US over allegations that Facebook and Instagram harmed children. It also requires Meta to introduce a series of new protections for teenage users.For Harry and Meghan, who have increasingly campaigned on online safety, the settlement represents progress but not an endpoint. They described it as a "positive step for everyone advocating for safer online spaces".The couple said the development showed that Meta and other social media companies "understand they are up against an immovable force of parents, survivors, and advocates who will not back down until we see change in how our young people interact with online spaces".Harry and Meghan's full statementThe Sussexes released their statement under the headline 'Meta To Pay Billions In Child Endangerment Settlement, Issues No Apology'. Their full statement read:"The historic trial against Meta over claims that its products endanger children has resulted in a settlement in which they will pay up to $17.1 billion. The settlement requires Meta to pay financial penalties for violating federal child privacy and states' consumer protection laws.By choosing to settle, the company paid to avoid yet another trial outcome that would force it into accountability. Because of the data-extraction business model Meta has used on our children and all users for years, it has more than the means to pay this settlement. Reports estimate Meta will make the equivalent of the $17 billion payout back in profit in the next 30 days.Alongside the settlement, Meta announced it will be making significant product changes for teens, including restricting platform use between 12 am and 6 am, stopping notifications during school hours, an optional chronological feed (as opposed to one based on algorithmically recommended interest-based content), and banning features that negatively impact mental health like beauty filters. Restricting teens' time on the platforms, if successfully enforced, would hit the company's business model, which relies on users spending as much time on the app as possible to see ads and generate data for advertisers.Meta's statement about these changes suggests it worked with 52 state attorneys to reach these product decisions, showing how unanimous the desire for change is across the United States. Their statement also emphasizes empowering parents with additional controls, which will need to be tested for effectiveness given Meta's history of placing responsibility for safety solely on parents.The statement fails to apologize or mention the billions it will pay out because of claims brought by the 29-state coalition and the 47 states plus the District of Columbia and territories included in the settlement. Their statement calls on YouTube and TikTok to join them in making similar design changes, and this agreement may also affect similar claims against other social media giants like Snap, YouTube, and TikTok.We hope it quickly sparks change from other tech leaders across the industry.This result clearly signals that Meta and social media companies understand they are up against an immovable force of parents, survivors, and advocates who will not back down until we see change in how our young people interact with online spaces. It is a positive step for everyone advocating for safer online spaces and at the same time – far from the end of the journey to a better online world.We celebrate with the parent and youth partners, legal and policy experts, and allies everywhere fighting for accountability. As always, we stand with them as they seek justice going forward, ensuring child online safety is built into any online space where our young people spend time."What Meta has agreed to changeThe settlement resolves claims brought by 47 US states accusing Meta of designing Instagram with features that could be addictive to children and teenagers and harm their mental health.The trial began last week in California and had been expected to include testimony from Zuckerberg before a federal court jury. The settlement is being viewed as one of the largest in state consumer protection history in the US.Under the agreement, Meta has unveiled protections and controls that will automatically apply to under-18 users on Instagram and Facebook, subject to court approval and only in participating US states.The changes include a default night-time block from midnight to 6am, muted notifications during school hours, hiding the number of likes and reactions on posts by default and blocking teenagers from using extreme makeup filters.Meta has also pledged to strengthen measures to prevent underage accounts from being created and to protect teenagers from harmful content.The changes, however, will not apply globally, including in the UK.The settlement will be paid in instalments over 10 years to the US states involved.Meta wants TikTok and YouTube involvedMeta has also called on TikTok and YouTube to introduce similar measures for teenage users.The company has warned that 30% of the settlement, worth approximately £4 billion, would only be paid if YouTube and TikTok agreed to pay the same amount and introduced measures such as one-hour daily limits, night mode and age-assurance systems.Meta chief legal officer CJ Mahoney said the company's new protections "will only work if all our peers join us"."Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution," he said. "As a parent, I'm proud of both the work Meta has done to protect kids historically, and of this new ground-breaking agreement."But its success depends on all other social media platforms following Meta's lead."Political reaction follows settlementThe settlement has also drawn a political response in the UK. The Tories said it demonstrated that social media companies "have turned a blind eye to the damage being done".Shadow education secretary Laura Trott said: "Social media companies can no longer be allowed to freely harm our children."They should not have unfettered access to children until they can prove their platforms are safe. Today's settlement shows that they are not."Trott has urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to "get on with" a social media ban for under-16s, which is set to come into force next year. She added: "Every further delay leaves more children exposed."The Molly Rose Foundation, established in memory of 14-year-old Molly from Harrow, London, who took her own life in 2017 after viewing harmful content, said the settlement "demonstrates that big tech can and should be held to account".Harry and Meghan's UK returnThe couple's intervention comes just a day after Harry and Meghan returned to Britain with Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet following six years in the US.They arrived at Birmingham Airport around noon after travelling from California on a private aircraft. They are understood to have travelled with their children on a Bombardier Global Express XRS from Van Nuys Airport in Los Angeles.The family were reportedly given no police protection on arrival, amid questions over whether taxpayers will ultimately pay for their security.Harry and Meghan are now setting up their home in Britain while planning to retain their properties in California and Portugal. They have said they intend to live as an "international" family.Their decision to return came as a surprise after they stepped back from the working monarchy in 2020 and later bought a home in Montecito.Harry, 41, and Meghan, 45, are expected to live in a non-royal residence outside London. Their children have reportedly been enrolled in schools in and around the Cotswolds and are due to start next week.The move follows a visit last month when the couple took Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five, to see King Charles at his Highgrove home for the first time in four years.The rest of the Royal Family is currently at Balmoral for its summer break.Meghan has 4.8 million followers on her personal Instagram account, while her business, As Ever, has around 900,000 followers.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: More social media safety should come with Meta changes, UN says
articles.summary: California's attorney general is now looking at TikTok and YouTube to enact teen safety features.
articles.body:
All of social media should be designed to be safe for children, the UN human rights chief has said after Meta settled a massive court case in the US.

Part of the deal the tech giant struck with almost all US states was to add more child safety measures - but Meta also called on TikTok and YouTube to add the same features.

The UN's high commissioner for human rights Volker Türk said governments needed to "step up rather than wait for courts and companies to act".

He added: "Children should not have to wait for a lawsuit to be safe online."

Türk said Meta's proposed changes, which include time limits and parental supervision controls, aligned with what he had been calling for - "but we're not there yet".

It included steps such as protecting data privacy and focusing on safer platform design, including better methods of verifying a user's age and not exposing such users to addictive design features.

However, the framework rejected the idea that outright bans on social media use for children was a good idea.

What does the Meta settlement mean for the UK? Five things we learned

Meanwhile, California Attorney General Rob Bonta - who represented one of the leading states in the Meta lawsuit - said he was "looking to ensure" TikTok adopted similar measures to Meta.

In agreeing on Wednesday to make various changes to end the states' lawsuit, Meta said they would only be truly effective "if all our peers join us."

Bonta told US News outlet CNBC he was "interested" in speaking to TikTok and YouTube, and that TikTok was "interested in speaking with us".

Neither company has responded to requests for comment since then.

Bonta added that he had communicated with Snap, another popular social media platform among younger users.

But he warned he was "willing to take additional steps" if they did not voluntarily make changes along the lines that Meta will be making.

On Tuesday, Meta agreed to pay up to $18bn (£13.3bn) to 48 US states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories.

articles.title: America’s first MD-granting medical school branch on tribal land will open in Arizona in 2027; 10 students a year will enter a 3-year programme on full tuition scholarships
articles.summary: US News: A new chapter in medical education is set to begin in Arizona in 2027, with the University of Arizona and Gila River Health Care (GRHC), the Gila Rive.
articles.body: A new chapter in medical education is set to begin in Arizona in 2027, with the University of Arizona and Gila River Health Care (GRHC), the Gila River Indian Community’s tribally operated healthcare system, announcing a long-term partnership to establish the nation’s first MD-granting medical school branch on the lands of a sovereign Tribal Nation.The University of Arizona College of Medicine – Phoenix Regional Medical Branch in Sacaton, Arizona, will train future physicians within a Tribal healthcare system while aiming to improve access to care in Tribal, rural and medically underserved communities.Beginning in July 2027, 10 students will be admitted each year to the University of Arizona College of Medicine – Phoenix’s three-year MD-granting Primary Care Accelerated Program at the Gila River Branch. The students will receive full tuition scholarships funded by GRHC, as per the official University of Arizona News report published on August 18, 2026.Students will split training between Phoenix and SacatonThe selected students will spend the first 18 months completing their foundational medical education in Phoenix. They will then relocate to Sacaton for the final 18 months of clinical education within the Gila River healthcare system.University of Arizona President Suresh Garimella said the initiative is designed to address some of the country’s most pressing physician shortages.“Tribal and rural communities have some of the nation’s greatest unmet primary care needs,” Garimella said.He added that the partnership would train physicians through an accelerated three-year MD programme while providing full scholarships to reduce the burden of student debt.“That is how you build a physician workforce that remains in the communities that need them most,” he said.Arizona faces growing need for primary care physiciansThe US continues to experience physician shortages, with rural and Tribal communities particularly affected. Arizona currently ranks No. 42 in the nation for primary care access, while its rapidly growing population has further increased demand for physicians.Research has shown that doctors are more likely to practise in the communities where they receive their training, making community-based medical education an important strategy for developing a long-term healthcare workforce.Instead of relying solely on large academic medical centres for medical education, the new Regional Medical Branch will place students directly within a community-based healthcare system.Students will work under faculty supervision and care for patients across different clinical settings. They will also gain an understanding of the historical, cultural and social factors that influence health in Native communities.Gila River Community hopes to create new opportunities for studentsStephen Roe Lewis, Governor of the Gila River Indian Community, described the partnership as an opportunity to make medical education more accessible to young people from the area.“This is a tremendous opportunity for our community and for the next generation of physicians,” Lewis said.“For too long, many of our young people who dreamed of becoming doctors had to leave home to pursue that goal. This partnership with the University of Arizona changes that. It gives them the opportunity to learn, train and build their careers right here in the Community, where they can make a real difference for the people they serve.”The University of Arizona and GRHC also believe the programme could encourage more Native American students to pursue medicine and create stronger pathways into Arizona’s physician workforce.GRHC commits more than $25 millionGila River Health Care has committed more than $25 million through 2034 to establish and support the Regional Medical Branch.The funding will cover faculty positions, student scholarships and educational infrastructure.Unlike traditional clinical rotations, students will become part of an operating healthcare system. They will work alongside physicians serving Native communities while gaining direct experience of the healthcare challenges affecting the population.The partners are also exploring the development of primary care residency programmes at GRHC. Such programmes could further support the long-term goal of retaining physicians in the Gila River Community and other underserved areas.Dr. Fredric Wondisford, dean of the University of Arizona College of Medicine – Phoenix, said the partnership could reshape how future physicians are trained.“This partnership challenges us to think differently about where and how physicians are educated,” Wondisford said.“Clinical excellence is shaped not only by scientific knowledge, but by understanding the communities physicians serve. By educating future physicians within a tribally operated healthcare system serving Native communities, we are creating a learning experience that cannot be replicated in a traditional academic medical center.”First-of-its-kind partnership aims to address physician shortageRobert Pablo, chairman of the Gila River Health Care Board of Directors, also highlighted the difficulty rural healthcare systems face in recruiting trained professionals.“There’s a real challenge for rural health hospitals to recruit trained professionals to come and work in their communities,” Pablo said.“We are very fortunate to launch this first-of-its-kind partnership between Gila River Health Care and the University of Arizona, which will establish a starting ground for these young doctors to jumpstart their careers.”The initiative builds on a similar partnership announced last year between the University of Arizona and Onvida Health in Yuma. The Regional Medical Branch is part of the university’s broader effort to expand community-based medical education across Arizona.The Association of American Medical Colleges projects that the US could face a shortage of up to 86,000 physicians by 2036, with Tribal and rural communities expected to be among those most affected.The University of Arizona, the Gila River Indian Community and GRHC believe partnerships between public research universities, sovereign Tribal Nations and community healthcare systems could play an increasingly important role in addressing the shortage.The new medical branch is expected to demonstrate how medical education can be brought directly into the communities that need doctors most, while simultaneously expanding educational opportunities and strengthening Arizona’s healthcare workforce.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Colombia's new president approves extradition of rebel leaders to US
articles.summary: It is a step towards ending a plan to stop violence by bringing rebel and criminal groups to the negotiating table.
articles.body:
Colombia's new right-wing president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has approved the extradition of five rebel armed group members who are wanted in the US on drug-related charges.

The move is a step towards ending a plan by his left-wing predecessor Gustavo Petro who tried to end the violence that has plagued Colombia for decades by bringing rebel and criminal groups to the negotiating table.

"Since the first day it was clear: peace cannot be a refuge for criminals nor a mechanism of impunity," de la Espriella wrote on X.

Speaking later he said Petro's peace plan had opened doors to criminals without securing their cooperation.

Critics of Petro's plan say his attempts to negotiate with a number of armed groups failed as members of the illegal organisations repeatedly broke ceasefires and walked away from the talks.

The five men facing extradition are members of dissident factions of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc), a left-wing rebel group that signed a peace deal with the government in 2016, and the Gulf Clan, thought to be Colombia's main drug trafficking cartel.

They are all wanted in the US on charges including drug trafficking, narco-terrorism and illegal weapons possession, among others. Only two of them are being held by Colombian authorities; three others remain at large.

The extraditions were approved by Petro in 2025, but they remained suspended because the men took part in the former president's peace efforts.

De la Espriella, who was sworn in earlier this month, has promised US President Donald Trump to escalate a war against drug trafficking in Latin America. Trump's administration has made targeting traffickers in the region a priority.

Colombia is the world's largest producer of cocaine and has long been one of Washington's closest allies in Latin America, but relations came under strain under Petro.

He openly challenged Washington's approach to combating drug trafficking and condemned the US military's deadly strikes on suspected drug-smuggling boats.

articles.title: 2 Air Canada Employees Arrested in Connection with Trafficking Cocaine and Cannabis at Montreal Airport
articles.summary: By switching baggage tags in secure airport zones, two Air Canada ground workers allegedly smuggled cocaine and cannabis through Montreal’s main hub
articles.body:
Two Air Canada employees are accused of trafficking drugs through secure areas of Montreal's main airport

Authorities allege the suspects used luggage tag switching to smuggle cocaine from Punta Cana and export cannabis there

Air Canada and airport officials are cooperating with authorities as the investigation continues

Two Air Canada employees have been arrested in connection with alleged cocaine and cannabis trafficking through one of Canada's busiest airports, authorities have announced.

According to a Wednesday, Aug. 26 press release from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP), the two suspects held various positions related to Air Canada ground operations at Montréal-Pierre Elliott Trudeau International Airport in Québec. Authorities allege the individuals "participated in a conspiracy" to bring and move luggage through secure areas of the facility to import cocaine and export cannabis.

RCMP said the investigation began in May 2026 when a Canada Border Services Agency operation intercepted 62.5 kg (138 lbs.) of cocaine concealed in backpacks carried on a flight from Punta Cana. During the course of the investigation, an additional 56 kg (123 lbs.) of cannabis was also seized.

Search warrants have been executed for two residences and a vehicle in the greater Montreal area, per the RCMP. A search is also being conducted, in coordination with the airline, within the employees' work base located in Dorval, Québec.

RCMP corporal Marie-Pierre Guertin tells Canadian outlet CTV News that the suspects had "access to secure zones."

"Being able to handle the luggage and go through the system where all the luggage with the tags and all that, it did give them easier access to be able to get the drugs in certain luggage to be able to export them," she said. "In this case...cocaine was imported from Punta Cana, and cannabis was exported to Punta Cana."

She added: "The way that the suspects worked, basically, is they switched tags of suitcases or luggage that is going to a certain destination to be able to transport the luggage containing the drugs."

However, Guertin did not specify how long the suspects have been involved in the alleged drug trafficking. She also did not share how many foreign countries were implicated or the monetary value of the alleged illegal goods.

In a statement shared with PEOPLE, a spokesperson for Aéroports de Montréal says they are cooperating with authorities in the investigation. They added: "It is important to note that access to the airport's restricted areas is governed by strict requirements, including screening and verification processes conducted by the appropriate authorities and employers, as well as ongoing controls carried out by various security partners, including the Canadian Air Transport Security Authority (CATSA) and Airport Security."

Due to the ongoing investigation, the spokesperson did not provide further comment.

Air Canada confirmed to PEOPLE it was informed of the arrests of two of its employees. The airline added that it is "cooperating fully" with RCMP and that the individuals have been suspended during the investigation.

RCMP said the two individuals arrested will be questioned and released pending further proceedings. Additional arrests may be made as additional evidence is analyzed and collected.
